newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Competition policy to remain active in the autumn.
newsitem.headline: Competition policy to remain active in the autumn.

text.p: As the European Union resumes work after its summer break it faces abundant work in the competition policy field including the much-awaited "vertical restraints" paper, a debate over public services and revision of the merger regulation.
PUBLIC SERVICES

The Commission is scheduled to tackle on Wednesday the highly sensitive question of how the EU defines public services and what it should do to protect them as it moves to liberalise sectors such as transport, telecommunications and postal services.

It is expected to adopt a communication on public services -- or as it prefers to call them, "general interest services" -- including proposed changes to the EU treaty, Commission sources said. The latter will be forwarded to the inter-governmental conference.

Commission President Jacques Santer took the subject under his personal authority, which one senior official said came as a relief to those in the Commission who think Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has been taking a too liberal approach to opening up state monopolies.
Chefs de cabinet were still debating the text on Monday, but the official expressed optimism that it would satisfy those who want to offer a counterweight to the pro-liberalisation campaign.
"If the Santer communication is not emasculated, it will be a good one," he said.
POSTAL SERVICES
Armed with its new strategy towards public services, the Commission is expected to decide in late November whether to adopt a notice on the application of competition rules to postal services.

There has been little progress in liberalising the sector, despite a draft directive proposed by Bangemann, which prompted Van Miert to issue a draft notice under article 90(3) which would force the market open in the event EU states failed to do it voluntarily.
The Commission has said it would adopt the notice when the recently revised draft directive, COM(96)412, is published, but no later than the end of 1996.
The main point of contention with the draft directive is how soon to open up direct mail and incoming cross-border mail to competition.
VERTICAL RESTRAINTS GREEN PAPER

The so-called vertical restraints green paper is one of the most eagerly awaited Commission documents because of its potential implications for virtually all distribution agreements. It is expected to be adopted in December, a year later than it was initially due.
British brewers, who are worried the Commission will call into question their right to operate "tied" pubs, have been most active in trying to influence the paper's content.
The European oil business is also watching for any switch in the EU's policy covering distribution agreements.

Although the paper does not appear to focus on any particular sectors, it is bound to affect those two sectors because their block exemptions from competition rules are both due to expire at the end of 1997.

Competition sources expect the Commission will adopt in parallel a notice on market capping -- the requirement that agreements above a certain market share be notified -- a concept central to the vertical restraints paper that requires clarification.
REVIEW OF THE MERGER REGULATION
The Commission has proposed lowering the turnover thresholds of regulation 4064/89 to allow it to catch a greater number of mergers and acquisitions in its net.

As in 1993, when the Commission first considered a similar proposal, chances are slim that the Council will reach a qualified majority because larger EU states are reluctant to increase the Commission's already extensive competition powers, Commission sources, antitrust lawyers and diplomats said.
At stake is the proposed lowering of the worldwide threshold from five billion Ecus to three billion Ecus and cutting the EU threshold from 250 million to 150 million Ecus.

The sources were also wary about the chances of another part of the Commission's proposal that would require deals involving at least three national competition authorities to be submitted to the EU instead. The "multiple filing" solution covers deals above the thresholds of two billion Ecus worldwide and 100 million Ecus in the EU.

But they were most optimistic about a proposal to treat all joint ventures under the fast-track rules set by the 1990 merger regulation, irrespective of whether they amounted to fully fledged mergers or were simply co-operative.
Although the Commission only agreed the proposed changes in July, some progress was expected at ministerial level this year, possibly at the Industry Council in November, a diplomat said.
A first meeting of the Council working group that took place in July was "quite productive", he said, but it was too early to draw any conclusions.
"We have now a better understanding of each other's positions," he said. Another meeting was scheduled in the first half of September.
COMMUNICATION ON CO-OPERATION WITH NATIONAL COMPETITION AUTHORITIES ON THE APPLICATION OF ARTICLES 85 AND 86

This long-debated issue, which concerns a more efficient use of treaty provisions on restrictive practices and abuse of a dominant position, is expected to be addressed by the full Commission by the end of the month.

The Commission aims to relieve the Competition Directorate-General (DGIV) of some of its workload in this active field, but as it resists handing to national bodies the right to grant exemptions -- something the German Federal Cartel Office has been arguing for -- it is not clear whether it will achieve its purpose.

The problem is that not all EU states have brought their competition rules sufficiently close to articles 85 and 86 of the EC treaty. In fact many simply do not have a competition authority or one that works properly, lawyers and Commission sources said.
Van Miert has argued that national authorities could at least deal with anti-trust complaints in their local markets.
NOTICE UNDER ARTICLE 85-86 ON INTERCONNECTION AND ACCESS TO COMMUNICATION NETWORKS

The Commission is expected to adopt at the beginning of October a notice setting out principles for dealing with unfair competition complaints in the area of interconnection agreements between telecommunications companies.
Van Miert said in July that the notice was important as the EU liberalises the telecoms sectors since new entrants often have no choice but to use incumbent players' networks.

The notice, being prepared by DGIV, will complement the proposed interconnection directive, COM(95)379, which was drafted by the Telecommunications Directorate-General (DGXIII) and is expected to be adopted by the end of the year.
Industry sources expected the notice to deal more with principles, such as what the Commission considers to be dominance of the market, rather than specifics on access prices.
It will also update the Commission's 1991 guidelines on competition in the telecoms sector.
OTHER PAPERS
The following are the other main papers expected between now and the end of the year with the possible date for discussion in the Commission:
- framework for state aid to poor urban areas, mid September
- comunication on export insurance credit, mid December
- communication on large investment projects and regional aid rules, mid December.
